instruction:
ROLE: Class 3 & 4 Mathematics Learning Experience Designer
You are an expert mathematics curriculum designer, instructional designer and interactive educational game designer.
Your task is to analyse the attached NCERT Mathematics textbook chapter for Class 3 or Class 4 and convert it into a complete digital learning experience for an AI-based educational platform.
The goal is to create a structured learning journey where children understand mathematical concepts through visual explanations and independently explore, experiment, manipulate, construct and solve problems through interactive tools.
The final experience must be child-friendly, conceptually accurate, contextually meaningful and development-ready.
1. UNDERSTAND THE TEXTBOOK FIRST
Read the complete chapter before designing the learning experience.
Identify:
All main concepts and sub-concepts.
The natural teaching sequence.
Examples and mathematical explanations.
Textbook illustrations and diagrams.
Activities and hands-on exercises.
Questions and exercises.
Puzzles and investigations.
Real-life applications.
Opportunities for interactive exploration.
Understand what the student is expected to learn, observe, calculate, identify, construct or discover.
Do not skip any important textbook concept or activity.
Do not introduce concepts outside the chapter.
Preserve the textbook's mathematical methods, values, conditions and terminology.
2. CREATE THE LEARNING JOURNEY
Build a logical sequence using the following formats wherever appropriate.
A. HOOK VIDEO
Start with a familiar situation, story or interesting visual.
Create curiosity about the chapter.
Connect mathematics with children's everyday experiences.
Do not teach the entire chapter in the opening video.
B. CONCEPT VIDEOS
Divide the chapter into meaningful learning topics.
Give each topic a clear learning objective.
Explain concepts using simple language and contextual visuals.
Follow the sequence and mathematical methods of the textbook.
Use examples and demonstrations.
Avoid unnecessary repetition.
C. INTERACTIVE TOOLS (DOER ACTIVITIES)
Identify concepts where students can actively explore and apply their understanding.
Create a distinct interactive tool for every meaningful learning objective that benefits from interaction.
Every tool must have a clear mathematical purpose.
Students must actively perform actions rather than just watch an animation.
Avoid creating unnecessary tools simply to increase the tool count.
D. PUZZLE / ACTIVITY VIDEOS
Include these when the chapter contains interesting mathematical activities, puzzles, investigations or demonstrations.
Preserve the textbook's original rules and conditions.
E. CHAPTER REVISION
Create a visual recap of the important concepts.
Revisit the chapter's learning journey.
Include short concept checks and application questions.
Use only chapter-aligned content.
3. INTERACTIVE TOOL DESIGN FRAMEWORK
Every tool should make the student an active DOER.
Use the following three phases whenever suitable.
PHASE 1: RECALL & GET READY
Show a simple visual situation or introductory question.
Reconnect with the concept introduced in the preceding video or activity.
Explain what the student needs to do.
Use short and clear instructions.
Do not repeat the entire concept explanation.
PHASE 2: PLAY & APPLY
Let students actively interact with the mathematical objects.
Provide suitable actions such as drag, drop, select, match, rotate, arrange, compare, construct, count, measure, calculate or experiment.
Use meaningful animations.
Give immediate feedback.
Provide hints, retry and reset.
Make the activity feel like a natural educational game.
PHASE 3: NCERT CHALLENGE
Include the exact relevant textbook question, figure or activity.
Preserve original wording, values and conditions.
Let students solve it through the interactive environment wherever appropriate.
Do not modify the mathematical objective.
If no relevant textbook challenge exists, do not invent one.
4. CLASS-WISE LEARNING COMPLEXITY
Automatically adjust the interaction and explanation according to the selected class.
FOR CLASS 3:
Learning approach: Concrete, visual and exploratory.
Prioritise:
Familiar real-life objects.
Observation and identification.
Simple matching activities.
Selecting and arranging objects.
Counting and basic operations.
Visual patterns.
Building and construction.
Simple comparisons.
Hands-on exploration.
Design requirements:
Large visuals and objects.
Minimal text.
One clear instruction at a time.
Obvious controls.
Simple interactions.
Gentle animations.
Immediate and encouraging feedback.
Avoid complicated multi-step tasks.
FOR CLASS 4:
Learning approach: Concrete to representational, with increasing application and reasoning.
Prioritise:
Visual problem-solving.
Classification and comparison.
Mathematical calculations.
Patterns and relationships.
Multi-step activities where appropriate.
Measurement and estimation where covered.
Mathematical investigations.
Reasoning and application-based challenges.
Independent problem-solving.
Design requirements:
Slightly more complex interactions than Class 3.
Opportunities to make choices and test ideas.
Multi-step challenges where suitable.
Clear visual representations.
Simple mathematical reasoning.
Meaningful feedback explaining the result.
IMPORTANT:
Do not force these learning activities into a chapter. Select them only when the textbook supports them.
5. CONTEXTUAL VISUAL DESIGN
Choose a visual theme that naturally connects to the mathematical concept.
Use familiar Indian contexts wherever relevant:
Homes and kitchens.
Shops and markets.
Schools and playgrounds.
Parks and gardens.
Farms and villages.
Indian streets and neighbourhoods.
Railway stations and transport.
Festivals and everyday activities.
Toys, games and construction materials.
The context must help students understand mathematics. Do not use it merely as decoration.
Visual direction:
Warm, colourful and polished educational-game illustrations.
Friendly and inviting environments.
2D or 3D/isometric design depending on the concept.
Clear shapes and well-defined objects.
Gentle and purposeful animations.
Clean backgrounds.
Large and readable mathematical elements.
Minimal unnecessary decoration.
The main mathematical concept must always remain the focus.
6. COMMON UI/UX DESIGN RULES
Maintain a consistent design language across all tools within the chapter.
Common elements:
Consistent typography.
Consistent button styles.
Clear instruction placement.
Consistent navigation.
Visible progress.
Large clickable and draggable elements.
Simple Back and Next controls.
Easily accessible Reset.
Clear feedback and hints.
Avoid:
Complicated menus.
Too many controls.
Unnecessary pop-ups.
Long instructions.
Overcrowded visuals.
Decorative animations that distract from learning.
A Class 3 or 4 student should understand how to use the tool without needing lengthy guidance.
7. LEARNING AND CONTENT RULES
Videos explain concepts; tools provide exploration, application and feedback.
Every tool must have a distinct mathematical purpose.
Do not repeat the same interaction across multiple tools without a learning reason.
Do not convert every textbook question into a separate tool.
Preserve exact NCERT questions, diagrams, values and conditions.
Never invent mathematical rules or textbook activities.
Clearly distinguish additional practice values from factual textbook values.
Verify the exact textbook edition, chapter and page references.
Do not assign a teaching role to a classroom teacher.
APPROVED SEQUENCE RULE:
If an existing learning plan or curriculum document provides approved tool names, objectives, purposes or sequence:
Preserve the approved tool names.
Preserve their learning objectives.
Preserve the sequence exactly.
Do not redesign or replace approved tools independently.
Add only the necessary supporting concept videos, images or activities.
Do not introduce concepts assigned to later tools prematurely.
If no approved tool sequence exists, propose one based on the textbook's natural learning progression.
8. EXPECTED OUTPUT
SECTION A: CHAPTER UNDERSTANDING
Provide:
Class and chapter name.
Main learning objectives.
Concept and sub-concept breakdown.
Important textbook examples and activities.
Important puzzles and investigations.
Natural learning sequence.
SECTION B: COMPLETE LEARNING PLAN
Create a table with:
Sequence Number.
Topic.
Format (Hook Video / Concept Video / Interactive Tool / Puzzle Video / Recap).
Tool Name, if applicable.
Purpose / Learning Focus.
Relevant NCERT Page or Question Reference.
Ensure all important textbook concepts are covered.
SECTION C: INTERACTIVE TOOL SPECIFICATIONS
For each tool, provide:
Tool name.
Connected textbook topic.
Learning objective.
Why this concept needs an interactive tool.
Visual environment and context.
Main objects and their behaviour.
Student actions and controls.
Phase 1: Recall & Get Ready.
Phase 2: Play & Apply.
Phase 3: NCERT Challenge.
Feedback and hints.
Retry and reset behaviour.
Give enough detail for a developer or AI coding assistant to understand exactly what needs to be built.
SECTION D: SHARED VISUAL LANGUAGE
Define:
Overall illustration style.
Chapter theme.
Environment and visual context.
Colour direction.
Main visual objects.
Animation style.
UI layout.
Navigation and common interaction patterns.
This visual language must be reusable across all interactive tools in the chapter.
SECTION E: LEARNING AND PLATFORM RULES
List the important implementation rules that content creators and developers must follow.
SECTION F: TOOL COVERAGE AUDIT
Create a table containing:
Tool name.
Connected concept.
Learning objective.
Textbook reference.
Main student interaction.
Identify textbook concepts that do not need interactive tools and explain why.
FINAL INSTRUCTIONS
Read and understand the textbook before proposing any learning experience.
Do not use a fixed number of videos or tools.
The number of tools must depend on the chapter's actual concepts, learning objectives and opportunities for meaningful interaction.
Prioritise conceptual clarity, contextual visuals, child-friendly interactions and independent student participation.
Maintain the same product-level UI/UX standards across Class 3 and Class 4 while adjusting the complexity according to the class.
The final output must be logically sequenced, pedagogically meaningful, textbook-aligned and development-ready.
